title: Book 5 — Terpsichore, Chapter 65
paragraphs: The Lacedaemonians would never have captured the sons of Peisistratus at all—for they had no intention of mounting a long blockade, and the others were well supplied with food and drink, so that they would have gone back to Sparta after only a few days' siege—had not something happened at this very moment which was unfortunate for one side and helpful to the other. The children of the sons of Peisistratus were captured while being secretly smuggled out of the country; and when this happened, all their plans were thrown into confusion, and they surrendered, receiving back their children on the terms the Athenians wanted: namely, that they should depart out of Attica within five days. After this they left the country and went to Sigeum on the Scamander, having ruled over the Athenians as a family for thirty-six years. These too were originally Pylians and sons of Neleus, descended from the same ancestors as the house of Codrus and Melanthus, who had earlier become kings of Athens though they had come from abroad. Hence too Hippocrates had given his son the name Peisistratus as a memorial, calling him after Peisistratus the son of Nestor.

So the Athenians were freed from their tyrants. And the deeds and sufferings worth narrating that they did or endured after liberation, up to the time when Ionia revolted from Darius and Aristagoras the Milesian came to Athens to ask for their help—these I will set forth first before going further.
